title: Sign Shop Letter Blocks
story: A sign shop builds shop-front lettering from pre-cut wooden blocks. Besides single letters, it keeps blocks for common letter groups like th, ing and bake, because one block is quicker to mount than four. The rule on the workbench: reading left to right, always grab the longest block that fits the next letters exactly. If no group fits, use a single letter.

Language models read text the same way. Before a model sees anything, a tokenizer cuts the text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary, and some tokenizers use this same longest-match-first rule. That is why a common word is often one token while a rare word breaks into several.
task: Write tokenize(text, pieces). Start at the first letter. At each position, find the longest string in pieces that appears in text starting exactly at that position. Add it to the result and move past it. If no piece matches, add the single letter at that position and move one step.
Return the list of tokens in order. Joined together they must spell text. An empty text gives an empty list.
constraints: text and pieces use lowercase letters a to z only. pieces may contain repeats.

examples.explanation: At position 0 both "ba" and "bake" fit; take the longer, "bake". At position 4, "ry" fits ("er" does not start there). The text is used up: ["bake", "ry"].
"th" at 0. At 2, "in" and "ink" fit, take "ink". At 5, "ing" fits. Result ["th", "ink", "ing"]. Notice greedy does not look ahead: it never considers "in" + "king", even though that would also work.
No piece starts with "z", so it becomes a single-letter token. Then "oo" fits. Result ["z", "oo"].

hints: In the first example, both "ba" and "bake" fit at position 0. If you scanned the pieces in the order given and took the first that fits, which would you pick?

The rule asks for the longest match, so the order of pieces must not matter. One option: check every piece at every position and keep the longest that fits. How many checks is that for a long text and a big vocabulary?
Flip the question around. Instead of asking every piece "do you fit here?", ask the text: "is the next 4-letter chunk a piece? The next 3? The next 2?" A set answers each question in one step.

Put the pieces in a set and note the longest piece length L. At position i, try lengths from min(L, remaining) down to 2, and take the first substring that is in the set. If none is, take one letter. Advance i by the length you took.
bruteForce: At every position, loop over all the pieces and check whether each one starts there, keeping the longest. With 10,000 letters and 1,000 pieces of up to 20 letters, that is up to 200 million character comparisons.

Most of that work is wasted: at any position only about 20 lengths are possible, and a set can say whether a given chunk is a piece in roughly one step. So check those few lengths instead of every piece.

js: * @param {string} text  the letters to cut up
py: def tokenize(text: str, pieces: list[str]) -> list[str]:

tests.note: piece longer than what is left
defeats searching anywhere instead of at the position

js: for (const p of pieces) longest = Math.max(longest, p.length);
// Try the longest possible piece first, then shorter ones.
len = Math.max(len, 1); // a single letter is always allowed
py: longest = max((len(p) for p in pieces), default=1)
# Try the longest possible piece first, then shorter ones.
while length > 1 and text[i:i + length] not in vocab:
length = max(length, 1)  # a single letter is always allowed
walkthrough: The greedy rule means you never undo a choice: at each position you take the longest piece that fits and move on. So the only real question is how to find that longest piece quickly.
Trace "bakery" with pieces ["ba", "bake", "ry", "er", "y"]. The set holds those five strings and the longest has 4 letters.
• i = 0: try "bake" (4 letters). In the set. Token "bake", i = 4.
• i = 4: only 2 letters left, so try "ry". In the set. Token "ry", i = 6.

Greedy is fast and predictable, but not always the fewest tokens: with pieces ab, abc, cd, the text "abcd" becomes "abc" + "d", not "ab" + "cd". Real tokenizers accept that trade-off. A trie of the pieces would avoid re-reading letters, but with pieces this short the set is simpler.
solution.timeWhy: At each of up to n positions you try up to L lengths, and building or hashing each substring costs up to L.
solution.spaceWhy: The set of V pieces, plus the output tokens.
solution.takeaway: Greedy longest-match: at each position try the longest candidate first and take the first one that is in a set. It is how many tokenizers split text, and the same idea works for any dictionary-based segmentation where you always want the biggest piece that fits.
